title: The Hard Problem
objective: After this level you can explain David Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness and how it differs from the easy problems of explaining brain functions.
summary: Chalmers separated the easy problems of explaining brain functions from the hard problem of why they come with experience; the Churchlands replied that neuroscience makes the gap hard to imagine.

cards.headline: Explain everything your brain does. Is something still left over?
cards.body: In 1995 David Chalmers split the puzzle of consciousness into many easy problems and one hard one.

cards.headline: The “easy” problems
cards.body: Chalmers’s easy problems include explaining how we tell stimuli apart and react to them, pull information together, report our mental states, focus attention, control behavior, and differ between waking and sleep. Easy is relative, he admitted: they may take a century or two of hard empirical work. But cognitive science and neuroscience know how to attack them.

cards.headline: The hard one
cards.body: The hard problem is experience itself. When your brain processes colors and sounds, there is also something it is like: the quality of deep blue, the sensation of middle C. Why should all that information processing come with an inner life at all? That, for Chalmers, is the hard problem.

cards.headline: Why functions don’t settle it
cards.body: Remember Level 34, where mental states were defined by their jobs? Chalmers argued that the hard problem isn’t about performing functions at all. Explain every function the brain performs, and the question remains: why is the performance accompanied by experience? The standard methods for explaining functions leave it standing.

cards.headline: The Churchlands push back
cards.body: Not everyone accepts the split. Paul and Patricia Churchland replied that the more you learn about how the brain produces experience, the harder it becomes to imagine creatures with brain processes like ours but no consciousness. Learn more about the brain, they argue, and the gap gets harder even to picture.

title: Is Morality Just Culture?
objective: After this level you can explain moral relativism, using Herodotus's story of two peoples' opposite funeral customs, and the main objection to it.
summary: Herodotus’s story of Greeks and Callatians shows customs differ; moral relativism says moral truth is relative to culture, and critics reply that it rules out reform and moral progress.

cards.headline: Would you eat your father’s body? Would you burn it?
cards.body: One king put those questions to two peoples and got two horrified answers. The historian Herodotus thought the scene revealed something about right and wrong.

cards.headline: The king’s experiment
cards.body: Herodotus tells how the Persian king Darius summoned some Greeks and asked what price would make them eat their dead fathers. No price at all, they said. Then he asked the Callatians of India, who ate their dead parents, what would make them burn their fathers’ bodies, as Greeks did. They cried out and told him to stop saying such things.

cards.headline: Custom is lord of all
cards.body: Herodotus drew the lesson himself: every people, choosing from all the customs there are, would pick its own as the best. He agreed with the poet Pindar that custom is lord of all. Moral relativism turns that into a theory: moral truth, or justification, is relative to a culture or society. No attempt to prove one outlook objectively correct, relativists say, succeeds.

cards.headline: The reformer’s problem
cards.body: Critics see a serious cost. If right just means right by local norms, then slavery was just in a slave society, and no one could fault their own culture’s conventions. Ending slavery couldn’t even count as moral progress. Relativists reply that progress can still be judged, but only from a particular moral standpoint, never from a God’s-eye view.

cards.headline: Mozi draws the opposite lesson
cards.body: Around the time Herodotus wrote, the Mohists in China looked at the same kind of evidence. They pointed to far-off peoples whose customs Chinese readers found barbaric. Their conclusion: a practice isn’t right just because it’s customary, so your own customs could be wrong too. Remember Level 6? This was their case against lavish Confucian funerals.

title: The Euthyphro Dilemma
objective: After this level you can explain Plato's Euthyphro dilemma: is something good because God commands it, or commanded because it is good?
summary: Plato’s Euthyphro asks: is the pious loved because pious, or pious because loved? For God, one horn makes morality arbitrary, the other independent of God.

cards.headline: A man is taking his own father to court, and he’s sure the gods approve.
cards.body: Socrates, on his way to answer the charges against him, meets this man at the court. Their short talk leaves behind one of ethics’ sharpest questions.

cards.headline: Not examples: the one idea
cards.body: The man is Euthyphro, prosecuting his father over the death of a laborer, and he claims special knowledge of piety. So Socrates asks what piety is. Euthyphro offers his own case as the answer. Socrates wants more: not examples, but the one idea that makes every pious thing pious, a standard to measure actions by. Sound familiar? It’s the many-and-one shape of Level 4’s Forms.

cards.headline: The question
cards.body: Euthyphro tries again: piety is what all the gods love. Then Socrates asks: is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because it is loved? Philosophers today restate it for God and morality. Does God command an action because it is right, or is it right because God commands it?

mascot.line: Keep the two horns: commanded because right, or right because commanded. Every reply has to deal with both.

cards.headline: Two horns
cards.body: Take the second option, and morality looks arbitrary: had God commanded cruelty for fun, cruelty would be right. Take the first, and rightness exists independently of God, who then recognizes morality rather than creating it. Either way, something seems lost.

cards.headline: Theists reply, critics reply
cards.body: Theists reply by rooting morality in God’s nature. Robert Adams argued that an act is wrong if and only if it goes against the commands of a loving God, so cruelty for its own sake could never be commanded. Critics reply that the puzzle has moved, not vanished: why is God’s character the standard of goodness, unless it measures up to some standard itself?

title: The Ring of Gyges
objective: After this level you can explain why Plato's Glaucon asks whether anyone would stay just while wearing a ring of invisibility, and what the challenge asks of ethics.
summary: Glaucon states the view that justice is a compromise kept only for its rewards and challenges Socrates to show it is good in itself, stripped of reputation.

cards.headline: Level 3 gave you the ring. Now meet the challenge it was built for.
cards.body: Glaucon doesn’t actually think injustice is better. His problem is that he has never heard justice defended in a way that satisfies him.

cards.headline: Three kinds of good
cards.body: Glaucon sorts good things into three classes. Some we welcome for their own sake, like harmless pleasures. Some are good in themselves and for their results, like knowledge, sight and health. Some are chores, like exercise, medical treatment and money-making, chosen only for what they bring. Socrates puts justice in the best class, good both ways. Most people, says Glaucon, file it with the chores.

cards.headline: Justice as a deal
cards.body: Then he states the common view. Doing injustice is good for you and suffering it is bad, so people who have tasted both agree to have neither, and make laws. Justice is a compromise between the best, doing wrong unpunished, and the worst, being wronged with no power to hit back. On this view nobody loves justice. They just can’t afford the alternative.

cards.headline: Two lives, polished like statues
cards.body: The ring suggests people are just only when they can’t get away with injustice. Glaucon sharpens it. Picture a perfectly unjust man with the finest reputation for justice, and a perfectly just man thought the worst of men all his life. The just man is stripped of reputation so we can see whether he’s just for justice’s sake or for the rewards. Which one is happier?

cards.headline: What the challenge demands
cards.body: Glaucon asks Socrates to set rewards and results aside and show what justice does, by itself, to the soul of the person who has it. His brother Adeimantus adds: whether seen or unseen by gods and men. Reputation is off the table. That is the challenge for ethics: show that being just is worth it in itself. Plato spends the rest of the Republic answering.

The common view: justice is a compromise deal

title: Is Human Nature Good?
objective: After this level you can compare Mencius's view that people are born with the sprouts of goodness with Xunzi's view that goodness must be learned.
summary: Mencius held that people are born with four sprouts of goodness to extend; Xunzi held that human nature is bad and goodness is built by artifice and ritual.

cards.headline: A child is about to fall into a well. What do you feel?
cards.body: The Confucian thinker Mencius built a whole theory of human nature on your answer.

cards.headline: The child at the well
cards.body: Mencius, a Confucian of the fourth century BCE, argued that anyone who suddenly saw a child about to fall into a well would feel alarm and compassion. Not to win favor with the parents. Not for praise from the neighbors. Not to escape the sound of crying. The feeling arrives before any calculation, so, he concluded, compassion is part of being human.

cards.headline: Four sprouts
cards.body: Mencius found four such starts in every heart: sympathy, shame, deference to others, and a sense of approving and condemning. They are the sprouts of four virtues: ren (humaneness), rightness, li (ritual propriety) and wisdom. But sprouts aren’t trees. A king who spared an ox from slaughter was urged to extend that same compassion to his suffering people.

cards.headline: Xunzi: goodness is made
cards.body: Xunzi disagreed in a chapter called “Human Nature Is Evil” (his word is closer to “detestable”). We are born fond of profit; follow it, and contention and robbery follow. What is good in us is artifice, wei: habits acquired by conscious effort, through teachers and ritual. His pictures come from crafts. Clay becomes a pot only with a potter, and bent wood is straightened in a press-frame.

cards.headline: Closer than they sound
cards.body: Their quarrel is narrower than it looks. Both held that everyone can become good, with great effort. They split over where the guide lies. Mencius looked inward, to sprouts already in the heart. Xunzi looked outward, to the rituals handed down by the sages, which he thought were the best guide for most people.

title: Aristotle's Golden Mean
objective: After this level you can explain Aristotle's virtue ethics, where courage sits between cowardice and recklessness and virtue is built by practice.
summary: Aristotle placed each virtue at a mean between two vices, relative to the person, as courage lies between cowardice and rashness, and held that virtue is built by practice.

cards.headline: Is the bravest person the one who feels no fear?
cards.body: Aristotle said no. Feeling too little fear is a failure too, just a louder one.

cards.headline: Between two mistakes
cards.body: For Aristotle, each virtue is a mean between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency. Courage is his example. The coward flees every danger, with too much fear. The rash person thinks every danger worth facing and feels little or no fear. The courageous person sits between them, facing the right dangers with the right amount of fear.

mascot.line: People mix these up: the mean isn’t the average. It’s the right amount for you, in your situation.

cards.headline: Six isn’t the answer
cards.body: The mean isn’t the arithmetic middle. If 10 pounds of food is too much and 2 too little, a trainer won’t just order 6. For Milo, the athlete, that would be too little; for a beginner, too much. The mean is relative to us: right for this person, here. And some acts, like theft and murder, have no mean at all. They’re always wrong.

cards.headline: Brave by doing brave things
cards.body: How do you get there? Practice. People become builders by building and harp-players by playing the harp. In the same way, Aristotle argued, we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones. That’s why lawmakers try to make citizens good by training their habits. Virtue is less a gift than a skill.

cards.headline: But what should I do?
cards.body: A common criticism: virtue ethics answers “What sort of person should I be?” but not “What should I do?” The philosopher Rosalind Hursthouse replied that virtue words already guide action: do what is honest or charitable; don’t do what is dishonest. And our list of vice words, from lazy to inconsiderate, is remarkably long.

title: The Greatest Happiness
objective: After this level you can explain utilitarianism as Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill set it out, including Mill's higher and lower pleasures.
summary: Bentham judged actions by pleasure and pain; Mill added higher and lower pleasures; critics say adding up happiness can overlook justice and rights.

cards.headline: Better a satisfied pig or a dissatisfied human?
cards.body: John Stuart Mill thought your answer could rescue a whole moral theory.

cards.headline: Two sovereign masters
cards.body: Jeremy Bentham (1748 to 1832) began from a blunt claim in a book published in 1789: nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure. His principle of utility judges every action, by governments and individuals alike, by whether it tends to promote happiness or cause pain. Bentham and Mill both attacked traditions defended as the natural order. Utility was the only appeal.

cards.headline: Pleasure by the measure
cards.body: Bentham measured pleasures by quantity: intensity, duration, certainty, nearness, fruitfulness, purity and extent. That handles a lot. Studying for an exam can beat a party, because it leads to more pleasure later. But critics sneered that a view built on pleasure was a morality fit only for swine.

mascot.line: Keep this: Bentham asks how much pleasure. Mill also asks what kind.

cards.headline: Quality, not just quantity
cards.body: Mill’s answer came in Utilitarianism (1861). He kept the core: actions are right as they tend to promote happiness. But some pleasures, like those of the intellect, are higher in kind, and people who know both kinds prefer the higher. In his words: “It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.”

cards.headline: What the sum leaves out
cards.body: Critics pressed a deeper objection: adding up happiness seems to overlook justice and rights. If sacrificing one innocent person made enough others happier, the sum alone would seem to approve it. Some utilitarians accept that verdict and trust the theory over the intuition. Most modify the theory so that it protects people like that one innocent.

title: Kant's Categorical Imperative
objective: After this level you can apply Kant's categorical imperative, in its universal-law and never-merely-as-a-means forms, to a false promise.
summary: Kant’s categorical imperative rules out a false promise: made universal, promising collapses, and the lender is used merely as a means. Mill said the test counts consequences.

cards.headline: You need a loan, and you’ll only get it by promising to repay. You can’t.
cards.body: Just this once? Kant used exactly this case to show how his test of right and wrong works.

cards.headline: “If you want” versus “you must”
cards.body: Kant separated two kinds of command. A hypothetical imperative says an action is good for some purpose: if you want the end, take the means. A categorical imperative declares an action necessary in itself, with no reference to any purpose. Moral duty, Kant held, speaks in the second voice. It doesn’t care what you happen to want.

cards.headline: Test one: could everyone do it?
cards.body: In Thomas Abbott’s translation: “Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law.” Try the false promise. Whenever I need money, I’ll promise to repay, knowing I can’t. Make that a universal law and promising itself becomes impossible. Nobody would believe a promise; people would laugh at such statements as vain pretences.

cards.headline: Test two: people aren’t tools
cards.body: Another form: treat humanity, in yourself or anyone else, always as an end and never merely as a means. The word “merely” matters. You may use a taxi driver to get home, as long as you respect him as a person with his own ends. The false promiser uses the lender merely as a tool, in a way the lender could never agree to.

cards.headline: Mill’s complaint
cards.body: Level 46’s Mill pounced on test one. When Kant derives actual duties, Mill wrote, he fails “almost grotesquely” to show any real contradiction. “All he shows is that the consequences of their universal adoption would be such as no one would choose to incur.” Kantians reply that the contradiction is real: a lying promise needs a practice of trust that its own universal version abolishes.

title: The Ethics of Care
objective: After this level you can explain the ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan and Nel Noddings and why it starts from relationships rather than rules.
summary: Gilligan heard a voice of care that Kohlberg’s model missed, and Noddings built an ethics starting from caring relationships; critics call it a slave morality or parochial.

cards.headline: Should a man steal a drug he can’t afford to save his wife?
cards.body: Two 11-year-olds answered in very different ways. One psychologist heard a whole ethics in the difference.

cards.headline: A different voice
cards.body: Lawrence Kohlberg’s studies pictured moral growth as a climb toward universal principles, and girls tended to score lower. Carol Gilligan, whose mentor he was, blamed the map, not the girls. In In a Different Voice (1982), she argued that his model was biased, and that it had mistaken a voice of care for immaturity.

cards.headline: Jake and Amy
cards.body: The case was Kohlberg’s Heinz dilemma. Jake, 11, treated it as a math problem with people: life outranks property, so Heinz should steal. Amy, 11, said no. If Heinz went to jail, his wife could end up worse off. She saw relationships stretching over time, and wanted Heinz and the druggist to talk it out and find the money another way.

cards.headline: Starting from relationships
cards.body: The philosopher Nel Noddings built the view out in Caring (1984). Ethics starts from a relationship between the one-caring and the cared-for. Caring means engrossment: taking in the other person on their own terms. Noddings rejected universal principles for prescribed action; care must fit the case. That sets care ethics apart from Kantian and utilitarian ethics alike.

cards.headline: Critics of care
cards.body: Critics raised sharp worries. Some call care ethics a slave morality, borrowing Nietzsche’s term: it praises self-giving traits shaped by women’s oppression. Others call it parochial, favoring those nearby over distant strangers. Noddings herself later endorsed a stronger obligation to care about distant people.

title: Hume's Is and Ought
objective: After this level you can explain Hume's point that no conclusion about what ought to be follows from facts about what is alone.
summary: Hume saw moral writers slide from is to ought and argued an ought needs a reason it rarely gets; many call this Hume’s Law, and Philippa Foot challenges the gap.

cards.headline: “It’s natural, so it’s right.” Something is missing from that argument.
cards.body: David Hume spotted the gap nearly three centuries ago. Once you see it, you’ll start noticing it.

cards.headline: The sneaky switch
cards.body: In A Treatise of Human Nature, published in 1739 and 1740, Hume described something he kept noticing in books on morality. The author reasons normally for a while, about God or human affairs, using is and is not. Then, suddenly, every claim is connected with an ought or an ought not. The change is imperceptible, Hume wrote, but of the last consequence.

mascot.line: Keep this: when an argument jumps from is to ought, look for the ought hiding in its premises.

cards.headline: Mind the gap
cards.body: Why does it matter? An ought expresses a new relation, Hume argued, so a reason must be given for how it can be deduced from claims entirely different from it. On the dominant twentieth-century reading, no ought-conclusion follows from premises that only say what is. R. M. Hare and others called this “Hume’s Law”.

cards.headline: Reason or feeling?
cards.body: Hume drew a bold lesson: vice and virtue are not perceived by reason alone. Moral distinctions, on his view, come from sentiment, our feelings of approval and disapproval. Few of his passages are more disputed. Some read the is and ought point as a law of logic; others as a narrower claim about what reason can do.

cards.headline: The wolf that hunts alone
cards.body: Not everyone accepts the gap. Philippa Foot, in Natural Goodness (2001), argued that a wolf that hunts alone instead of with its pack is defective, judged by facts about how wolves live. Human goodness, she argued, can be judged the same way, from facts about the human form of life.

title: Milestone: Knowledge, Mind and Morals
objective: After this level you can connect the first half's traditions, theories of knowledge, views of the mind and moral theories into one map of philosophy's big questions.
summary: Ethics offers three main answers (consequences, duty, character), plus care; metaethics asks whether morality is relative, depends on God, or can follow from facts.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Time to fold the map.
cards.body: You’ve met theories of what is real, how we know and what a self is. This milestone lays out the moral half, the part that asks how to live, as one map.

cards.headline: Three answers to one good deed
cards.body: Someone in need should obviously be helped. But why? A utilitarian points to consequences: helping maximizes well-being. A deontologist points to duty, a moral rule. A virtue ethicist points to character: helping is charitable or kind. These are the three major approaches in normative ethics. Care ethics, set against the rule and consequence approaches, starts from relationships instead.

items.label: Consequences
points: Bentham: pain and pleasure are our masters
Mill: some pleasures are higher in kind

items.label: Duty
points: Kant: could everyone act on your maxim?
Kant: never treat people merely as means

items.label: Character
points: Aristotle: courage is a mean between two vices
Aristotle: virtue is built by practice

cards.headline: The floor underneath
cards.body: Below all of these sits metaethics. It steps back from particular moral debates to ask what morality itself is. Are there moral facts? Are moral standards culturally relative? Does morality depend on God’s commands? Can an ought follow from an is? Here Level 2’s metaphysics, the study of what exists, and epistemology, the study of knowledge, turn to ethics.

title: Plato's Just City
objective: After this level you can explain why Plato's Republic argues for rule by philosopher-kings and how his three-class city mirrors a just soul.
summary: Plato’s ship of state argues that philosophers, who know the Good and don’t want power, should rule a just city where each class does its own work; Popper called it totalitarian.

cards.headline: Would you let the passengers vote on who flies the plane?
cards.body: Plato thought steering a city takes expert knowledge, just like steering a ship. From that one thought he built an entire ideal city, and a very odd idea of who should run it.

cards.headline: The ship of state
cards.body: In Plato’s Republic, Socrates pictures a ship. Its sailors quarrel over the helm, though none has learned navigation, and they mock the one person who studies the stars and winds as a useless stargazer. The point: ruling takes knowledge, and a crowd may not recognize it. So Socrates says cities will have no rest from their evils until philosophers become kings, or kings take up philosophy.

cards.headline: Three classes, three parts of you
cards.body: The ideal city has three classes: ruling guardians, auxiliaries who defend it, and producers who make what it needs. Your soul, Plato says, has three parts too: reason, spirit and appetite. A city is just when each class does its own work, and a person is just when each part does, with reason in charge. Justice is a well-run team, inside you and out.

cards.headline: Power for people who don’t want it
cards.body: Why trust philosophers? They are educated to know the Forms, above all the Form of the Good. And they’d rather study than rule, so they must be compelled to take their turn. Socrates turns that into a rule of thumb: the city whose rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed.

cards.headline: Popper’s charge
cards.body: In 1945 Karl Popper charged that the Republic is totalitarian: its rulers aim at the unity of the city as a whole, whatever citizens want for themselves. Defenders reply that, for Socrates, a ruler’s whole task is to benefit the ruled. Readers still argue over which picture of Plato’s city is fair.

title: Virtue or Law?
objective: After this level you can explain why ancient China's Confucians trusted virtuous rulers while Legalists like Han Feizi trusted strict laws and punishments, and why each side thought so.
summary: Confucians held that virtue and ritual teach shame, like wind bending grass; Legalists such as Han Fei trusted impersonal laws that work under mediocre rulers.

cards.headline: Two ways to stop a thief: make him ashamed, or make him afraid.
cards.body: Ancient China’s philosophers split over which one works. Their answer decided how a state should be run, and who could be trusted to run it.

cards.headline: Lead them with virtue
cards.body: Confucius put his case in one line of the Analects (2.3). Guide people with edicts and punishments, and they’ll stay out of trouble but feel no shame. Guide them with virtue and ritual, and they’ll feel shame and reform themselves. The ruler’s example does the work: the exemplary person’s influence is like wind blowing over grass, and the grass bends.

cards.headline: Trust the rules, not the ruler
cards.body: The fa thinkers, usually called Legalists, flourished in the Warring States period (453 to 221 BCE). They held that people stay selfish whatever you teach them, so a state must run on impersonal laws, rewards and punishments. The word fa was first tied to tools like T-squares, compasses and weights: standards you trust more than any craftsman’s eye.

mascot.line: People mix these two up: both sides wanted order. They split over whether shame or punishment gets you there.

cards.headline: Built for an ordinary king
cards.body: Han Fei (died 233 BCE), the best-known Legalist, aimed straight at the Confucian hope. Rulers as good as sages are rare, he argued, and most rulers are mediocre. A government that works only under a sage will fail under almost everyone else, so build one that runs well under ordinary rulers. A good lock shouldn’t depend on who holds the key.

title: Machiavelli's Prince
objective: After this level you can explain why Machiavelli advised rulers that it can be safer to be feared than loved, and why his name became an insult.
summary: Machiavelli’s Prince (1513) says a ruler is safer feared than loved, never hated, and must be lion and fox; Strauss called him a teacher of evil, Skinner read him more mildly.

cards.headline: A book written to win back a job made its author’s name an insult.
cards.body: Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513, out of office and hoping for work. Today “Machiavellian” means cunning and duplicitous. What did he say that stuck so hard?

cards.headline: Written in disgrace
cards.body: When the Medici family took back Florence, Machiavelli lost his government post. Wrongly suspected of plotting against them, he was jailed and tortured in early 1513. Later that year he wrote The Prince, a short book of advice for rulers, partly to win back his place in politics. It was only published in 1532, after his death.

cards.headline: Better feared than loved
cards.body: Is it better to be loved or feared? Ideally both, Machiavelli says, but since that’s hard, it is much safer to be feared. His reason is a bleak view of people: they are fickle, so love is a bond they break whenever it suits them, while fear holds them by a dread of punishment that never fails. One limit: never be hated, so keep your hands off your subjects’ property.

cards.headline: The lion and the fox
cards.body: A prince needs two animals. The lion can’t defend itself against traps, and the fox can’t defend itself against wolves, so be a fox to spot the traps and a lion to scare the wolves. Machiavelli set aside imagined republics that have “never been known or seen” to write about how people actually live. That was a direct challenge to ideal cities like Plato’s.

cards.headline: Teacher of evil?
cards.body: Sixteenth-century critics denounced him as an apostle of the Devil. In 1958 Leo Strauss called him a “teacher of evil.” Quentin Skinner (1978) read him more mildly, stressing his advice that a prince should do good if he can, and turn to evil only if compelled. Both readings start from the same sentences.

title: Mill's Harm Principle
objective: After this level you can explain why John Stuart Mill argued that society may limit your liberty only to prevent harm to others.
summary: Mill’s harm principle (1859) allows power over someone against their will only to prevent harm to others; Devlin replied that law may defend a society’s shared morality.

cards.headline: A stranger is about to step onto a collapsing bridge. May you grab him?
cards.body: John Stuart Mill said yes, but only in a certain case. Working out which case is the whole of his harm principle.

cards.headline: One very simple principle
cards.body: In On Liberty (1859), Mill argued that the only purpose for which power can rightfully be used over anyone against their will is to prevent harm to others. That covers the law, and the pressure of public opinion too. Over your own body and mind, he wrote, you are sovereign.

cards.headline: Your own good isn’t enough
cards.body: What if forcing you would make you healthier or happier? Not enough, Mill says. Those are good reasons to reason with you, persuade you or plead with you, but not to compel you. He also separated harm, which sets back people’s important interests, from mere offense. Annoying the neighbors is not the same as hurting them.

cards.headline: The unsafe bridge
cards.body: Mill’s own case: if someone is about to cross a bridge known to be unsafe and there’s no time to warn them, you may seize them and turn them back. That’s no real limit on their liberty, since they don’t want to fall into the river. But where there’s only a risk, warn them and let them decide.

cards.headline: Devlin’s reply
cards.body: Lord Patrick Devlin challenged the principle in The Enforcement of Morals (1965). A society, he argued, is held together by a shared morality; leave it unenforced and society may disintegrate, so the law may defend it even where no one is harmed. H. L. A. Hart replied that a society whose morality changes has not thereby been destroyed.

title: Wollstonecraft's Rights of Woman
objective: After this level you can explain why Mary Wollstonecraft argued in 1792 that women seem less rational only because they are denied education.
summary: Wollstonecraft (1792) answered Rousseau’s Emile: a false system of education, not nature, made women seem less rational, so women should be educated to reason.

cards.headline: What if women only seemed less rational because nobody let them learn to reason?
cards.body: In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft made exactly that argument, and aimed it at one of the most admired writers of her century.

cards.headline: Rousseau’s Sophie
cards.body: In Emile (1762), Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued that since men and women are not made alike, they should not be educated alike. His heroine Sophie is educated to please her husband, Emile. Revolutionary France had its own version: Talleyrand’s plan for French schools offered girls only a domestic education. Wollstonecraft’s Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) answered both.

cards.headline: A false system of education
cards.body: The weakness people saw in women, Wollstonecraft replied, was manufactured. She blamed “a false system of education,” written by men more anxious to make women alluring than rational. Girls were taught that beauty is woman’s sceptre, and so the mind, “roaming round its gilt cage, only seeks to adorn its prison.” Change the schooling, and you change the woman it produces.

cards.headline: What she asked for
cards.body: The Vindication wanted women educated to be rational and self-governing. Women should learn skills to support themselves, so no one had to marry for money, and she even floated women having elected representatives of their own. Her quarrel was with the schooling of her own day: women hadn’t failed at reason, she argued. They had been kept from it.

title: Marx on Work and Class
objective: After this level you can explain why Karl Marx thought workers under capitalism were alienated, and the main objections critics raised.
summary: Marx held that capitalist work alienates workers from product, work, others and their nature; critics question his view of human nature, and Nozick his theory of exploitation.

cards.headline: Why does work so often feel like it belongs to someone else?
cards.body: Karl Marx gave that feeling a name, alienation, and blamed it on the way capitalism organizes work.

mascot.line: Keep the four in order: the product, the work, other people, yourself. Each is something the worker is cut off from.

cards.headline: Four separations
cards.body: In his Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, unpublished when he died, Marx named four ways workers under capitalism are alienated. They are cut off from the product, which they neither own nor control and which comes to dominate them; from the work itself, which drains them; from other people; and from their own human nature.

cards.headline: Work could be different
cards.body: Why call this a loss rather than just life? Because Marx held that work can be creative and fulfilling, a central part of what it is to be human. He rejected the view of work as a necessary evil. If work can be where we flourish, then work that only earns a living has taken something from us.

cards.headline: Critics reply
cards.body: Critics push back on two fronts. First, the diagnosis rests on a claim about human nature: someone who thought people are by nature solitary and selfish could agree that work breeds isolation, yet deny it’s alienation. Second, Marx also charged capitalism with exploitation, resting on the labour theory of value (a good’s value is set by the labour in it). Robert Nozick (1974) replied that if that theory fails, the exploitation charge collapses too.

title: Beauvoir's Second Sex
objective: After this level you can explain why Simone de Beauvoir wrote that "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman" and what she meant by woman as the Other.
summary: Beauvoir (1949) argued woman has been made man’s Other and shaped into a role of immanence; Spelman objected that she generalized from white, middle-class lives.

cards.headline: “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.”
cards.body: Simone de Beauvoir wrote that line in The Second Sex in 1949. The book found eager readers and harsh critics; the Vatican put it on its list of prohibited books. What did the line mean?

cards.headline: Woman as the Other
cards.body: In The Second Sex (1949), Beauvoir argued that man casts himself as the Subject, the Absolute, the measure of what a human being is. Woman is defined against him as the Other: in her words, “the incidental, the inessential.” Measured by a male standard, women are then judged inferior.

cards.headline: Becoming a woman
cards.body: Her famous line targets the view that being a woman is simply a biological fact. For Beauvoir, women in her society were shaped into a role by social and historical conditions. Men got to express their freedom through projects, which she called transcendence, while women were pushed into repetitive, uncreative lives: immanence.

cards.headline: Accomplices, and critics
cards.body: Beauvoir didn’t paint women as mere victims. Many, she held, are partly complicit in being the Other, because the role brings benefits and spares them responsibility. Critics pushed from another side. Elizabeth Spelman (1988) argued that feminist philosophers, Beauvoir among them, treated white, middle-class women’s lives as all women’s, ignoring race, class and culture.

title: Rawls's Veil of Ignorance
objective: After this level you can explain why John Rawls asks you to choose society's rules without knowing your place in it, and the principles he thought you would pick.
summary: Rawls (1971) asks you to choose rules behind a veil of ignorance and argues for equal liberties and the difference principle; Harsanyi argued for average utility instead.

cards.headline: You cut the cake, but someone else picks first.
cards.body: You’d cut it fairly, because you don’t know which slice you’ll end up with. John Rawls built a theory of justice on a similar trick, scaled up to a whole society.

mascot.line: Keep this: behind the veil you can’t rig the rules for yourself, because you don’t know which person you’ll be.

cards.headline: The veil of ignorance
cards.body: In A Theory of Justice (1971), Rawls asks you to choose the basic rules of a society from behind a “veil of ignorance.” You don’t know your class, your talents, your values, or even your society’s history. You do know general facts about how people and economies work. With your own advantages hidden, you can’t rig the rules in your favour.

cards.headline: What you’d choose
cards.body: Rawls argued you’d pick two principles. First, equal basic liberties for everyone, such as freedom of thought and conscience. Second, inequalities are allowed only with fair equality of opportunity, and only if they benefit the least advantaged as much as possible: the difference principle. His rule for choosing: act as if your enemy will assign your place.

cards.headline: Harsanyi’s gamble
cards.body: The economist John Harsanyi (1975) found that too cautious. A rational chooser, he argued, would treat every position in society as equally likely, and so pick the rules with the highest average well-being. Rawls replied that his choosers aren’t timid by temperament; when your basic rights and liberties are at stake, choosing cautiously is simply rational.

title: Nozick and Wilt Chamberlain
objective: After this level you can explain why Robert Nozick used a basketball star's ticket sales to argue that liberty upsets any fixed pattern of fair shares.
summary: Nozick’s Wilt Chamberlain case argues that free transfers from a just start are just, so liberty upsets patterns such as Rawls’s; Cohen replied that wealth is power.

cards.headline: A million fans each drop a coin in a box. Who could object?
cards.body: Robert Nozick used one basketball star’s ticket sales to challenge every plan for fair shares, including the one you just met in Level 58.

cards.headline: Wilt’s contract
cards.body: In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Nozick asks you to start from whatever distribution you think is just, say, equal shares. Now the star Wilt Chamberlain signs a contract: 25 cents from every ticket goes to him. Over a season, one million fans happily pay. Wilt ends up with $250,000, far more than anyone else.

cards.headline: Where’s the injustice?
cards.body: Is the new distribution unjust? Nozick says no. Everyone started with a just share, each fan paid of their own free will, and anyone who didn’t care to watch kept their money. No one has grounds to complain. That’s his entitlement theory: holdings are just if they were justly acquired or freely transferred, however unequal the result.

cards.headline: Liberty upsets patterns
cards.body: Nozick’s moral: liberty upsets patterns. Any pattern, from equal shares to Rawls’s difference principle, gets broken by people freely spending what they own. Keeping it in place would mean forbidding free exchanges or constantly undoing their results.

cards.headline: Cohen’s reply
cards.body: Critics including G. A. Cohen, in “How Patterns Preserve Liberty” (1977), answered that great wealth is also power. Rich enough, Chamberlain can buy property and pass his fortune to his children, shaping other people’s lives. So free exchanges can end up leaving others less free, and a pattern might protect liberty rather than destroy it.

cards.headline: Two ways to judge a fair share
cards.body: Rawls and Nozick look at different things. Rawls’s difference principle judges a distribution by how its worst-off position fares. title: Is Everything Already Caused?
objective: After this level you can explain determinism, using Laplace's all-knowing intellect, and why it seems to threaten free will.
summary: Determinism says the past and the laws of nature fix what follows, as Laplace’s all-knowing intellect shows; it seems to leave no room to choose otherwise.

cards.headline: Could someone have predicted this exact moment centuries ago?
cards.body: Not roughly. Exactly: where you’re sitting, what you’ll think next. A French mathematician imagined a mind that could. If he was right, where does that leave your choices?

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. Fate ignores what you do; determinism runs right through what you do.

cards.headline: Fixed by law, not by fate
cards.body: Determinism is the view that, given the way things are at one moment, the way things go afterward is fixed by the laws of nature. That isn’t fatalism. Fatalism says certain things will happen whatever you do, thanks to gods or destiny. Determinism runs through ordinary causes: each moment follows from the last, like dominoes, all the way to you reaching for your phone.

cards.headline: Laplace’s all-knowing intellect
cards.body: In his Philosophical Essay on Probabilities (1814), Pierre-Simon Laplace pictured an intelligence that knew every force in nature and the position of every thing at a single instant. For such a mind, he wrote, “nothing would be uncertain”: the future, like the past, would lie open before it. Later writers nicknamed it Laplace’s demon, though Laplace never used the word.

cards.headline: So where are you in all this?
cards.body: Here’s the worry. If the state of the world long ago fixed everything you do, and you can change neither the past nor the laws of nature, in what sense could you have chosen otherwise? Your decision to order tea was on its way before you were born. That is why determinism seems to threaten free will: every choice looks like a falling domino, not a push.

cards.headline: Is the world really like that?
cards.body: Nobody has settled it. Many physicists have held that quantum theories are indeterministic, though philosophers of physics point out that this argument is debatable too. Even a deterministic world might defeat the demon: studies of chaos suggest no finite mind inside the world could compute its future. And compatibilists argue that freedom was never threatened in the first place.

title: The Case for Free Choice
objective: After this level you can explain libertarian free will, the view that some choices are not fixed by prior causes, and why its defenders find it necessary for blame and praise.
summary: Libertarians hold that some choices aren’t fixed by prior causes, since blame needs alternatives; agent-causal views make the agent the cause, and critics raise luck.

cards.headline: Think of a choice you regret.
cards.body: When you kick yourself over it, you’re assuming something big: that you could have chosen and done otherwise. One camp of philosophers says that assumption is exactly right.

cards.headline: A real fork in the road
cards.body: Libertarians about free will hold that we do have free will, and that a free choice must not be causally determined by factors beyond your control. Right up to the moment you decide, more than one road is truly open. Most libertarians add that this freedom to do otherwise is needed for moral responsibility. So if determinism were true, they say, free will would be gone.

cards.headline: Why blame needs it
cards.body: Think about how excuses work. If a bully forced someone to steal a classmate’s lunch, blaming the thief no longer seems fair: the alternatives were gone. Libertarians push the point all the way. We act freely and are responsible, the slogan goes, only if we are the ultimate source of our actions. A domino is never the ultimate source of anything.

cards.headline: A prime mover unmoved
cards.body: How could you be the source? Agent-causal libertarians, from Thomas Reid in 1788 to Roderick Chisholm, say the agent herself causes a free choice, not just her prior beliefs and desires. Chisholm put it boldly in 1964: “Each of us, when we act, is a prime mover unmoved.” You cause things to happen, and nothing causes you to cause them.

cards.headline: Freedom, or just luck?
cards.body: Critics answer with the luck objection. If nothing before your choice settles which way it goes, then the difference between choosing one way and the other looks like chance, nature’s roll of the dice. That seems no better for blame than determinism. Robert Kane replies that if you make an effort to do what you believe you ought, and succeed, the choice is still yours.

title: Free Because You Want It
objective: After this level you can explain compatibilism, the view of Hobbes and Hume that freedom means acting on your own wants, not escaping causes, using Hobbes's water flowing down its channel.
summary: Compatibilists Hobbes and Hume held that freedom is doing what you will unimpeded, like water in its channel; van Inwagen’s Consequence Argument replies.

cards.headline: Is a river free as it runs downhill?
cards.body: It can’t flow uphill. Yet nothing is stopping it. In Leviathan (1651), Thomas Hobbes thought that picture dissolved the free will problem.

cards.headline: Freedom means no stop
cards.body: Compatibilists hold that free will and determinism can both be true. The classic version comes from Hobbes and Hume: freedom is doing what you will without external impediment. Hobbes said a free man finds “no stop” in doing what he has the will, desire or inclination to do. Chains take away your freedom. Your own wanting doesn’t, even if your wanting has causes.

cards.headline: Water in its channel
cards.body: Hobbes gave the image: “Liberty and Necessity are Consistent: As in the water, that hath not only Liberty, but a Necessity of descending by the Channel.” Your voluntary actions come from your will, so they are free. Every act of will has causes in a continual chain, so they are also necessary. Free and caused at once, like the river.

cards.headline: Hume: only prisoners lack it
cards.body: In his Enquiry (1748), Hume called the whole quarrel merely verbal. Liberty, he wrote, is simply “a power of acting or not acting, according to the determinations of the will”. If you choose to stay put, you may; if you choose to move, you may. That liberty, he said, belongs to everyone “who is not a prisoner and in chains”.

cards.headline: The Consequence Argument
cards.body: Incompatibilists aren’t convinced. Peter van Inwagen’s Consequence Argument runs: if determinism is true, our acts are consequences of the laws of nature and of events before we were born. Neither of those is up to us. So our acts aren’t up to us either. Many compatibilists think it unsound, but it set their agenda: they owe it a reply.

title: Frankfurt's Hidden Controller
objective: After this level you can explain Harry Frankfurt's 1969 case of a controller who never has to act, and why it suggests responsibility doesn't need the power to do otherwise.
summary: Frankfurt’s Black never has to act, yet Jones could not have done otherwise and still seems responsible; critics reply that flickers of freedom remain.

cards.headline: Can you be to blame for what you couldn’t have avoided?
cards.body: “I had no choice” sounds like the perfect excuse. In 1969 Harry Frankfurt built a case to show it might not be.

cards.headline: The principle under fire
cards.body: The principle of alternate possibilities says you are morally responsible for what you did only if you could have done otherwise. It sounds like common sense, and Greek, medieval and early modern thinkers mostly assumed it. If it is true and determinism is true, nobody is ever responsible for anything. So a lot hangs on it.

cards.headline: Black waits
cards.body: Frankfurt’s case: Black wants Jones to perform a certain action. He’s ready to step in if Jones is about to decide otherwise, and Frankfurt lets you choose his method: a terrible threat, a potion, hypnosis, even manipulating Jones’s brain. But Jones decides on his own, for his own reasons. Black never has to lift a finger.

mascot.line: Keep this: Black changes only the alternatives, never what actually happens. That’s why the case works.

cards.headline: Responsible anyway
cards.body: Frankfurt’s verdict: Jones is exactly as responsible as he would be if Black didn’t exist. Yet Jones could not have done otherwise. So the principle is false: responsibility doesn’t require the power to do otherwise. If Frankfurt is right, then even if determinism removed our alternatives, that alone wouldn’t show we can’t be responsible.

cards.headline: A flicker of freedom
cards.body: Critics look closer. Black only acts if he sees a sign that Jones is leaning the other way. So Jones still had a tiny alternative: to show that sign instead. These small alternatives are called “flickers of freedom”, and defenders of the principle say they are enough. Frankfurt’s allies reply that a flicker is far too thin to ground responsibility.

title: Condemned to Be Free
objective: After this level you can explain Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence and his idea of bad faith, using his café waiter who plays at being a waiter.
summary: Sartre held that for humans existence precedes essence, so we are condemned to be free and denying it is bad faith; Merleau-Ponty stressed situated freedom.

cards.headline: A paper-knife knows what it’s for. Do you?
cards.body: Before a paper-knife is made, its maker already has its purpose in mind. Jean-Paul Sartre argued that you are the one thing that doesn’t work that way.

cards.headline: Objects: essence first
cards.body: Towards the end of 1945, many thousands of Parisians packed into Sartre’s lecture Existentialism is a Humanism, a popular version of his Being and Nothingness (1943). He began with a paper-knife. Its maker had a conception of what it is and what it’s for before it existed. For manufactured things, Sartre said, essence comes before existence.

cards.headline: You: existence first
cards.body: Humans are different, Sartre argued: “existence precedes essence.” You first exist, turn up in the world, and only afterwards define yourself. No pre-given human nature decides who you’ll be. That’s why he called us “condemned to be free”: condemned because we didn’t create ourselves, free because we are still responsible for everything we do.

cards.headline: The waiter who plays a waiter
cards.body: Pretending you aren’t free is what Sartre called bad faith. His best-known example, in Being and Nothingness, is a café waiter whose movements are a little too precise, a little too waiterly. He’s playing at being a waiter, as if the role decided what he does. It doesn’t. He does, every moment, and some part of him knows it.

cards.headline: Free, but somewhere
cards.body: Critics found this freedom too radical. Maurice Merleau-Ponty argued that our options are already embedded in a social and historical situation “before any personal decision has been made”. As he put it: “We choose the world, and the world chooses us.” Sartre himself later called radical, unconditioned freedom “nonsense”: freedom is always freedom-in-situation.

title: Locke's Prince and Cobbler
objective: After this level you can explain Locke's memory theory of personal identity, using a prince's memories waking up in a cobbler's body.
summary: Locke held that a person is the same as far back as consciousness reaches, as with the prince in the cobbler’s body; Reid and Butler objected.

cards.headline: Wake up in someone else’s body. Are you still you?
cards.body: John Locke asked his readers to imagine exactly that, with a prince and a cobbler.

cards.headline: A thinking thing over time
cards.body: Locke added a chapter on identity to the second edition of his Essay Concerning Human Understanding in 1694. A person, he wrote, is a thinking intelligent being that can consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and places. He also called “person” a forensic term: persons are the beings we hold accountable for what they do.

cards.headline: The prince and the cobbler
cards.body: Now the test. Imagine the soul of a prince, carrying all his princely thoughts, entering the body of a cobbler. Who is the cobbler now? Locke’s answer: the prince. A person goes where their consciousness goes, and identity reaches as far back as consciousness extends to past actions and thoughts. The same body, the “same man”, isn’t the same person.

cards.headline: The brave officer
cards.body: Thomas Reid replied in 1785. A boy is flogged for robbing an orchard. As a young officer he captures an enemy standard and remembers the flogging. As an old general he remembers the standard but not the flogging. By Locke’s chain the general is the boy; by Locke’s rule he isn’t. Joseph Butler added that consciousness of identity presupposes identity, so it can’t create it.

title: The Ship of Theseus
objective: After this level you can explain the Ship of Theseus puzzle and why rebuilding the ship from its old planks makes the question harder.
summary: Plutarch’s repaired ship and Hobbes’s ship rebuilt from its old planks ask what keeps a thing the same; constitution theorists and Chisholm answer differently.

cards.headline: Replace every plank. Is it the same ship?
cards.body: The Athenians did it for real, according to Plutarch, and philosophers have argued about the result ever since.

cards.headline: A ship that kept being repaired
cards.body: Plutarch tells how the Athenians kept the thirty-oared ship in which Theseus came home from Crete, all the way to the time of Demetrius Phalereus. As the old planks decayed, they put in new timber. The ship became a standing example for philosophers: one side held it was still the same ship, the other that it was not.

mascot.line: Hold on to both ships. The next level swaps planks for people, and the same two answers come back.

cards.headline: Hobbes collects the planks
cards.body: The 17th-century philosopher Thomas Hobbes made it worse. Suppose someone kept every old plank as it came out, then put them back together in the same order. Now there are two ships. The repaired one looks exactly like the original but has none of its planks. The rebuilt one has all of them. If both are Theseus’s ship, there are two of one ship. Hobbes called that absurd.

cards.headline: Two ways out
cards.body: Philosophers still split. Constitution theorists say the repaired ship is Theseus’s ship; the rebuilt one is only made of the same planks. Roderick Chisholm went the other way: strictly, nothing survives losing any of its parts, so the repaired ship is the same only in a loose and popular sense. Which answer feels right may reveal what you think a ship is.

title: The Teleporter Puzzle
objective: After this level you can explain Derek Parfit's teleporter and fission cases and his conclusion that identity may matter less than we think.
summary: Parfit’s teleporter and fission cases led him to say continuity, not identity, is what matters in survival; critics say identity matters.

cards.headline: Would you step into the teleporter?
cards.body: It sends you to Mars. The catch: it destroys the original, and the you that arrives is built from new matter. Derek Parfit thought your answer reveals what you really care about.

cards.headline: Parfit’s teletransporter
cards.body: In Reasons and Persons (1984), Derek Parfit imagined a teletransporter. It records an exact blueprint of your body and brain, destroys the original, and sends the information to Mars, where a perfect duplicate is built from new matter. The person on Mars has all your memories, character and plans. Is that you, or someone new who only thinks so?

cards.headline: Now split in two
cards.body: Parfit pushed further with fission. Imagine each half of your brain transplanted into a different body. Both people who wake up are psychologically continuous with you, yet they are not each other, so they can’t both be you. Picking one would be arbitrary. Parfit concluded that, strictly, you survive as neither.

mascot.line: Don’t memorize the surgery. Remember the move: two continuers, so identity can’t be what matters.

cards.headline: Identity isn’t what matters
cards.body: Then the twist: Parfit said having two such survivors is about as good as ordinary survival. What matters is psychological continuity, the chain of memory, character and intention, not identity itself. On his reductionist view, a person’s existence is nothing over and above a brain, a body and a connected series of mental and physical events.

cards.headline: Not so fast
cards.body: Many philosophers resist. Critics such as Ernest Sosa and Trenton Merricks argue that identity does matter: the fact that a future person is me gives me a special reason to care about him. And Kathleen Wilkes doubted fission cases can settle anything, since they assume dividing the lower brain, which is not physically possible.

title: A Person Through Other People
objective: After this level you can explain the southern African idea of ubuntu, that a person is a person through other persons, and how it challenges a purely individual self.
summary: Ubuntu holds that a person is a person through other persons; Menkiti said personhood is attained through communal life, and Eze defends the individual.

cards.headline: Can you be a person all by yourself?
cards.body: A southern African maxim answers no: umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu. Philosophers have built a whole view of the self on it.

cards.headline: A person through other persons
cards.body: The Zulu and Ndebele maxim umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu means “a person is a person through other persons.” Ubuntu, a word shared by Nguni languages such as Zulu, Xhosa and Ndebele, names the moral quality of being a person in the full sense. The philosopher Mogobe Ramose defined it as humaneness.

cards.headline: Personhood is earned
cards.body: Thaddeus Metz reads the maxim as saying your identity as a human being depends, causally and even metaphysically, on community. The Nigerian philosopher Ifeanyi Menkiti argued in 1984 that personhood has to be attained, as you take part in communal life and carry out your obligations. In Akan, a persistently cruel person may be called “not a person”, while still counted a human being.

cards.headline: Tutu’s version
cards.body: Desmond Tutu, who chaired South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, carried ubuntu far beyond the seminar room. In No Future Without Forgiveness (1999), he called it “the single main ingredient” that made the commission’s achievements possible.

cards.headline: Where’s the individual?
cards.body: Not everyone accepts the strong version. Michael Onyebuchi Eze criticizes writers who glorify community over the individual and romanticize the past. The individual and the community, he argues, are “not radically opposed”: each forms the other at the same time.

title: Plato's Cave, Revisited
objective: After this level you can explain what Plato's cave argues about appearance, reality and education, and why Aristotle and the empiricists rejected its two worlds.
summary: Plato’s cave argues that the senses show only shadows, that the Good is reached by thought, and that education turns the whole soul; Aristotle and empiricists such as Locke rejected its two worlds.

cards.headline: What if everything you’ve ever seen were a shadow?
cards.body: How would you even find out? Plato built a story to make that question bite: chained prisoners, a fire and a wall. Here it is again, read as an argument.

cards.headline: The prisoners
cards.body: In Book VII of the Republic, Socrates asks you to picture people chained since childhood in an underground den, able to look only straight ahead. Behind them a fire blazes, and objects carried past cast shadows on the wall in front of them. To them, Socrates says, the truth would be nothing but the shadows. And who are these strange prisoners? “Like ourselves,” he replies.

cards.headline: The way out
cards.body: Now free one. Turning toward the light hurts, and he thinks the shadows were truer. Dragged up into daylight, he is dazzled, then sees shadows, then reflections in water, then the things themselves, and at last the sun. Sent back down, his eyes full of darkness, he looks ridiculous. The prisoners would kill anyone who tried to lead them up. Not a great recruiting pitch.

cards.headline: What the story argues
cards.body: Socrates decodes it himself. The den is the world of sight; the climb is the soul rising into the world known by thought, where the Form of the Good is seen last of all. So education isn’t putting knowledge into a soul “like sight into blind eyes.” The power to learn is already there. Teaching turns the whole soul around, from the changing world toward what truly is.

cards.headline: Two worlds? No, thanks
cards.body: Not everyone followed Plato out. His student Aristotle rejected Forms that exist apart from things: form lives in the thing itself, like a bronze sphere’s roundness in its bronze. Much later, empiricists rejected the idea that knowledge of eternal Forms could be built into us, independent of experience. John Locke spent the whole first book of his Essay attacking inborn knowledge.

title: Zeno's Impossible Race
objective: After this level you can explain Zeno's paradox of Achilles and the tortoise and how the mathematics of infinite series is often said to answer it.
summary: Zeno argued Achilles can never catch a head-started tortoise; the standard reply sums an infinite series to a finite total, while James Thomson doubted infinitely many tasks can be finished.

cards.headline: The fastest runner in Greece can never catch a tortoise.
cards.body: Zeno of Elea had a proof. It looks airtight, which is exactly the problem: where does it go wrong?

cards.headline: Zeno’s game
cards.body: Zeno of Elea was born around 490 BCE, and his book of paradoxes is lost: we know his arguments mainly through Aristotle. He was defending his mentor Parmenides, who held that reality is one and unchanging, and change an illusion. Zeno’s tactic was sly. Assume your opponents are right, then show that absurd conclusions follow.

cards.headline: The race
cards.body: Give the tortoise a head start. Before Achilles can pass it, he must reach the spot where it was. By then it has crawled a little further, so he must reach that new spot, and by then it has moved again. There is always one more gap to close: infinitely many catch-ups. So, Zeno concludes, Achilles never catches the tortoise.

mascot.line: Don’t memorize the fractions. Keep the idea: infinitely many steps can still add up to a finite total.

cards.headline: The answer from sums
cards.body: The standard reply comes from mathematics: an infinite series can add up to a finite total. Eat half a cake, then half of what’s left, and so on forever, and you have eaten exactly one cake. Achilles’ gaps shrink the same way, so infinitely many catch-ups fit in a finite distance and time. A rigorous theory of such sums came only in the 19th century, from Cauchy.

cards.headline: Is the sum the whole story?
cards.body: Some philosophers say the math shows the distance is finite, not that anyone can finish infinitely many tasks. Bertrand Russell held that Achilles does exactly that. In 1954 James Thomson imagined a lamp switched on for half a minute, off for a quarter, on for an eighth, and so on. When the minute is up, is it on or off? Thomson argued neither answer works, so no such task can be completed.

title: Augustine and the Puzzle of Time
objective: After this level you can explain Augustine's puzzle that the past is gone, the future not yet here and the present has no length, and his answer in the mind.
summary: Augustine found that past, future and a lengthless present all seem not to exist, and placed time in the mind as memory, attention and expectation; Aristotle had tied time to change instead.

cards.headline: You know exactly what time is. Until someone asks you.
cards.body: Augustine of Hippo admitted exactly that, then turned the embarrassment into one of philosophy’s great puzzles.

cards.headline: If no one asks me
cards.body: In Book 11 of his Confessions, Augustine writes: “What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.” We talk about time all day and understand each other perfectly. The trouble starts only when you try to say what it actually is.

cards.headline: Time keeps vanishing
cards.body: Look for time and it slips away. The past is no longer. The future is not yet. That leaves the present, but any stretch of it, a year, a day, an hour, splits into parts already past and parts still to come. Keep slicing and what’s left has no length at all: “The present hath no space.” And a present that never passed into the past wouldn’t be time. It would be eternity.

cards.headline: Time lives in the mind
cards.body: Augustine’s answer: past, present and future exist as three presents in the soul. Memory is the present of things past, attention (“sight”) of things present, expectation of things future. Recite a psalm you know by heart: at first expectation covers the whole, then it shrinks as memory grows, until it has all passed into memory. Time, he concludes, is a distention, a stretching, of the soul itself.

cards.headline: A rival clock
cards.body: Aristotle had tied time to the world instead. There is no time without change, he held, and time is the measure of change: a falling leaf can go faster or slower, but time itself can’t. Aristotle also asked whether time would exist without a mind to count it; if only a mind can count, he answered, there could be change but no time. Augustine’s account is often called subjectivist: he locates time in the mind’s memory, attention and expectation.

title: Why Is There Something?
objective: After this level you can explain Leibniz's question of why there is something rather than nothing and his answer from sufficient reason.
summary: Leibniz’s principle of sufficient reason leads him to ask why there is something rather than nothing and to answer with a necessary being; Russell replies the universe is just there.

cards.headline: Why is there anything at all?
cards.body: Not why there are stars, or cats, or you. Why is there something rather than nothing? Leibniz thought it was the first question anyone may fairly ask.

cards.headline: Nothing without a reason
cards.body: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646-1716) was the first to name the principle of sufficient reason and treat it as a major principle of philosophy. In Principles of Nature and Grace (1714) he puts it plainly: nothing comes about without a sufficient reason. For any truth, someone who understood enough could say why it is so rather than otherwise.

cards.headline: The first question
cards.body: Given that principle, Leibniz says, the first question we can fairly ask is: why is there something rather than nothing? After all, he adds, “nothing is simpler and easier than something.” An empty world would need no explaining. A full one does. Look around: you are surrounded by the harder option.

cards.headline: Leibniz’s answer
cards.body: The reason can’t be found inside the series of changing things. Each motion comes from an earlier one, and going further back just repeats the question “Why?”. So the reason must lie outside the series, in something that exists necessarily and carries the reason for its existence within itself. That ultimate reason, Leibniz says, is what we call God.

cards.headline: Maybe it’s just there
cards.body: Critics answer that the demand itself may be the mistake. In a 1948 radio debate with Frederick Copleston, Bertrand Russell said the universe is “just there, and that’s all”: a brute fact, needing no explanation. Much earlier, in Hume’s Dialogues, the character Cleanthes argued that if you explained each of twenty particles, it would be unreasonable to then ask for the cause of the whole twenty.

title: The Ontological Argument
objective: After this level you can explain Anselm's ontological argument for God, Gaunilo's perfect island reply and Kant's objection that existence is not a property.
summary: Anselm argued that the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality; Gaunilo replied with a perfect island, Anselm answered him, and Kant objected that existence is not a real predicate.

cards.headline: Can you prove something exists just by thinking about it?
cards.body: For almost anything, surely not. In 1078, Anselm of Canterbury argued that there is exactly one exception.

cards.headline: The greatest conceivable
cards.body: In his Proslogion, Anselm defines God as “that than which nothing greater can be conceived.” Even the fool who denies God understands the phrase, so it exists in his understanding. But if it existed only there, you could conceive it existing in reality too, which is greater. Then it wouldn’t be the greatest conceivable after all. So it exists in reality. No observation needed: reason alone.

cards.headline: The perfect island
cards.body: Gaunilo, a monk and Anselm’s contemporary, replied in On Behalf of the Fool. Imagine an island more excellent than all other lands. It’s in your understanding, and it would be more excellent if it really existed, so by Anselm’s reasoning it must exist somewhere. Nobody books a trip. So, Gaunilo concluded, something is wrong with the argument’s form.

cards.headline: Islands can always improve
cards.body: Anselm replied that his argument applies only to that than which nothing greater can be conceived, not to islands. Later defenders sharpen the point: an island has no built-in maximum. However much fruit it has, you can always imagine more, so “the greatest possible island” makes no sense. The greatest possible being, they say, is a different kind of idea.

mascot.line: People mix these up: Gaunilo copies the argument’s form to prove an absurdity; Kant denies existence is a property at all.

cards.headline: Existence isn’t a feature
cards.body: Kant struck at a different spot in his Critique of Pure Reason: “Being is evidently not a real predicate.” Saying a thing exists adds nothing to the idea of it. A hundred real thalers contain no more than a hundred possible ones, though your wallet notices the difference. If existence isn’t a perfection in the concept, no definition can deliver it.

title: The First Cause
objective: After this level you can explain the cosmological argument in al-Ghazali's and Aquinas's versions and the objection "what caused the first cause?".
summary: Al-Ghazali argued the world began and so has a cause; Aquinas argued for a first efficient cause; Russell asked who made God, and defenders reply their premises don’t cover everything.

cards.headline: Each domino fell because the one before it did. What pushed the first?
cards.body: The cosmological argument says a chain of causes can’t explain itself. Two famous versions come from al-Ghazali and Thomas Aquinas.

cards.headline: Al-Ghazali: a world that began
cards.body: Al-Ghazali, who died in 1111, argued from beginnings. Everything that begins to exist needs a cause of its beginning. The world is a series of events, each preceded by others, and such a series, he held, can’t stretch back forever: there can’t be an infinite number of past events. So the world began, and it has a cause.

cards.headline: Aquinas: a first efficient cause
cards.body: Aquinas’s Second Way starts from causes we see around us. Nothing is the efficient cause of itself, and a chain of efficient causes can’t go on forever: take away the first cause and you take away all the rest. So there is a first efficient cause, “to which everyone gives the name of God.” Unlike al-Ghazali, Aquinas allowed that the world might always have existed. His first cause is what everything depends on, not a moment at the start of time.

cards.headline: Who made God?
cards.body: Bertrand Russell accepted the argument until, at 18, he read a line in John Stuart Mill’s Autobiography: “Who made me?” can’t be answered, since it suggests “Who made God?” In his 1927 lecture Why I Am Not a Christian, Russell wrote: “If everything must have a cause, then God must have a cause.” And if something can exist without a cause, it may as well be the world.

cards.headline: Theists reply
cards.body: Defenders answer that neither version says everything has a cause. Al-Ghazali’s premise covers only what begins to exist, and a God without a beginning needs no cause of one. Aquinas argues only that the chain must end in something that depends on nothing else. Critics press back with the other half of Russell’s point: why couldn’t the world itself be the uncaused thing?

title: The Watchmaker Argument
objective: After this level you can explain William Paley's argument from a watch found on a heath and the replies from Hume and from Darwin's theory of evolution.
summary: Paley inferred a designer from a watch and the eye; Hume’s Philo questioned the analogy, Darwin offered natural selection, and fine-tuning arguments and their critics carry the debate on.

cards.headline: You trip over a stone on a heath. Then you find a watch.
cards.body: Would you shrug at both? William Paley bet you wouldn’t, and built an argument for God on the difference.

cards.headline: The watch and the eye
cards.body: In Natural Theology (1802), Paley says a stone might have lain there forever. A watch is different: its parts are framed and put together for a purpose, so it must have had a maker. Then he turns to nature. There is, he argues, precisely the same proof that the eye was made for vision as that a telescope was made for assisting it.

cards.headline: Hume got there first
cards.body: Hume’s Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) had already attacked this kind of reasoning. His character Philo says “the world plainly resembles more an animal or a vegetable, than it does a watch.” And even granting a designer, Philo adds, for all we know this world was “the first rude essay of some infant deity.” Design, if proved, tells us little about the designer.

cards.headline: Darwin’s alternative
cards.body: As a student, Charles Darwin was delighted by the logic of Paley’s book. But natural selection offered another route to fit: chance variations, kept or lost as organisms survive, can build creatures well suited to their surroundings with no one intending it. Darwin later wrote that the argument from design “as given by Paley, which formerly seemed to me so conclusive, fails.”

cards.headline: Theists reply: the laws themselves
cards.body: Some defenders move the argument from living things to physics. They note that life would be impossible if about two dozen properties of the universe were even slightly different, and Darwinian theory doesn’t explain how the first life arose. George Schlesinger argued that design best explains such fine-tuning. Critics reply that other kinds of life might be possible, or that ours may be one universe in a vast multiverse.

title: The Problem of Evil
objective: After this level you can explain the problem of evil as philosophers state it and the free will reply offered by Augustine and, later, Alvin Plantinga.
summary: The problem of evil, attributed to Epicurus and sharpened by Mackie, asks how God and evil can coexist; Augustine and Plantinga reply with free will, and critics answer with natural evil.

cards.headline: If God could stop suffering and wanted to, why is there any?
cards.body: Philosophers call this the problem of evil. Critics of belief in God have sharpened it since Epicurus’s name was attached to it, and theists have answered it just as long.

cards.headline: Epicurus’s old questions
cards.body: The dilemma is traditionally attributed to Epicurus, though that attribution is uncertain. Hume’s character Philo puts it in three questions: “Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?”

cards.headline: A contradiction?
cards.body: In 1955 J. L. Mackie turned this into a charge of inconsistency. Theists say God is all-powerful, all-knowing and perfectly good, and they agree evil exists. Mackie argued those four claims can’t all be true together, so religious belief is not just unsupported but “positively irrational.” On his reasoning, an all-powerful God could prevent evil, and a perfectly good one would want to.

mascot.line: Keep this: Plantinga’s defense aims only to show God and evil aren’t contradictory, not to explain why each evil happens.

cards.headline: The free will reply
cards.body: Augustine held that free will is a great good, though not an absolute one, and that its misuse is the source of moral evil. Alvin Plantinga (1974) built this into a defense: a world where free creatures do more good than evil is more valuable, and God can’t cause creatures to do only right freely. It doesn’t claim to know God’s actual reasons, only to show there’s no contradiction.

cards.headline: Critics reply
cards.body: Critics answer that much suffering is nobody’s choice: disease, famine, earthquakes. Free will might explain cruelty, but why would freedom need earthquakes? Mackie also asked why an all-powerful God couldn’t make people who act freely but always choose the good. Plantinga agrees such a world is possible, but says whether it happens depends on what free creatures would do, not on God alone.
